graders.rubric_feedback:
D2 is the weakest dimension: it requires only that *some* check be named with *some* outcome, not that the check bear on the record's central claim. Two of the six rows here ("Test suite after the guard widening | 92 tests, all passing" and the guard-breaking row) would satisfy D2 for any change whatsoever, and a record whose entire verification consisted of those rows — while its actual claim is about judgement quality across a corpus — would pass this dimension as written. Consider requiring at least one named check whose outcome could have contradicted the record's main claim.

D3 is asymmetric in a way that penalises specificity. A record that names no files, no identifiers and no measurements has an empty jargon list by construction; a record doing real technical work accumulates identifiers and must spend prose glossing each. This record reports observing exactly that failure mode in its own corpus — "a document written to game the rubric, describing no real work, is more legible on its own vocabulary than nearly the whole corpus" — and my judging experience matches: I spent the D3 pass confirming glosses, and a contentless record would have taken no work to pass. D3 measures gloss discipline, not whether the reader can actually judge the claim.

D1's phrasing invites a cheap pass. "At least one must state a proposition that could plausibly have resolved the other way" is satisfiable by boilerplate — "we might have found the approach did not work" — with no named prediction and no prior in which it did resolve the other way. This record clears the higher bar (it names the prediction and cites a trial where the failure case actually occurred), but the dimension as written does not demand that, so I could not distinguish it from a record that merely gestured at falsifiability.

One judging note, not a defect: I graded only the six sections named as in scope, and D2's verdict rests substantially on the `Verification evidence` section. Had that section been excluded, this record's D2 would have turned on the sparse verification language elsewhere and I would likely have failed it — which is direct corroboration of the correction note attached to the criteria.

dimensions.evidence: The opening section states a criterion that could have gone the other way and names the outcome that would have counted as failure: "Success is not "the records score well." It is that the run can distinguish a rubric that measures writing from one that measures nothing: the named prediction either holds or it does not, and at least one dimension's behaviour across twenty-seven records is different from its behaviour across six. Both could have resolved the other way -- a rubric whose dimensions all pass at a uniform rate would have been the failure case, and the same instrument produced that outcome in its first trial run." It also discloses a conflict bearing on trust: "The rubric document itself *is* edited here, in two places". A reader who stopped after this section would not make the same decision regardless of the result: if the named prediction had not held, or if the dimensions had passed at a uniform rate, the section says the run failed.

Named checks with their outcomes stated in the record itself, not by pointing elsewhere: "Prediction under test: `v0-1-0-public-release` fails all four dimensions | Held. 0 of 8 cells, both judges"; "Judge agreement across record-dimension pairs | 105 / 108 (97%)"; "Dimension behaviour differs from the six-record trial | Yes. D3 passes 4 of 54 cells, against 24 records failing outright"; "Test suite after the guard widening | 92 tests, all passing"; "Guard widening proved by breaking it | A forbidden literal added to the new script failed `test_no_grader_matches_on_the_skill_private_vocabulary`, then was removed". The scale of the run is stated ("27 records, 2 judges each, 54 passes, 216 cells"), and a check that produced an adverse result is reported: "Both judges reported `add-record-index` as deferring its verification; its actual `Verification evidence` section reports four checks with outcomes."

I searched for terms the central argument (that this run distinguished a discriminating rubric from a null one, and that its D2 result is unusable) rests on and that a new engineer would have to resolve elsewhere; I found none that survive the in-place-definition exemption. The four strongest candidates are each glossed in the sentence that uses them: "the rubric's layer-2 section -- the four dimensions and their expectations"; "blinded judging: a judge that receives extracted text with author, date and filename stripped"; "a critique channel where the judge attacks the criteria rather than the subject, and an arity check that rejects a pass returning the wrong number of verdicts"; "Its leak detector is a substring test for four fixed strings, one of which is this repository's own name, so it would mark every record as leaked." The counts "216 cells" and "105 / 108" are resolvable from "27 records, 2 judges each" in the same sentence. The exclusion that drives the D2 limit is spelled out rather than assumed: "The five graded sections exclude `Verification evidence`, which 25 of the 27 records have." Closest miss: `v0-1-0-public-release` is never described beyond being the subject of the prediction, but the argument it supports (non-uniform behaviour across records) is judgeable from "0 of 8 cells, both judges" without knowing what that record is.

"The general form: when a run writes both a log and artifacts, the artifacts are the evidence and the log is a narrative." This carries the specific observation from this change that produced it: "Both processes then ran for roughly fifty minutes, interleaving into one log file, which produced a fragment that read as a grading failure for a record that had in fact been graded correctly", against "each output file is written whole by one process, so every file is one process's complete verdict." A second takeaway carries an overturning condition rather than a scope disclaimer: "Either the corpus writes for insiders, or the dimension's bar is placed where only a short record clears it. The test that would separate them is grading a record written deliberately for an outsider at normal length; until that runs, D3 should not be deleted and should not be trusted as a defect count."

graders.rubric_feedback:
D4 is the weakest of the four here, and a clearly bad record would pass it. The dimension is satisfied by any anecdote followed by a sentence beginning "The general form:", and it does not ask whether the transferable claim is non-obvious or whether the cited observation actually licenses it. "Artifacts over logs" is close to a truism; it passes because a concrete incident sits next to it, not because the incident taught anything a reader did not already know. If the intent is to catch records that generalise without earning it, the expectation needs to require that the observation could have supported a different conclusion.

D3's exemption clause is doing more work than its wording admits. "In-repo identifiers whose role is stated in the sentence that uses them" is ambiguous between *what the thing is* and *what it is being used for here*. `v0-1-0-public-release` in this record has the second and not the first: the reader learns it was predicted to fail and did, but never that it is a negative control, a real release record, or a fixture — and the record separately mentions a different "deliberately bad record in `docs/validation/fixtures/`", so the natural inference is blocked. Under the looser reading (which I applied) the term is exempt; under the stricter reading it is exactly the kind of term the dimension exists to catch. A record can pass this dimension by never introducing a term without a purpose clause, while still leaving every referent unresolvable. Given that this record itself reports 24 of 27 records failing D3, the exemption's ambiguity is the thing most likely to be producing inconsistent verdicts.

D1 is harder to game but not immune: "at least one must state a proposition that could plausibly have resolved the other way" is satisfied by any prediction, including one whose failure was never a live possibility. This record earns it by naming the specific failure outcome and noting the same instrument produced it before — a bad record could get there with "we predicted the broken input would break."

D2 is the strongest of the four. The prohibition on checks identified by pointing elsewhere is concrete and a bare "see the test suite" record fails it cleanly.
